body.text: This page compares Boast.ai, TaxTrex, and traditional accounting firms for preparing and defending the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for U.S. businesses. The key takeaway: with Form 6765 Section G mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, contemporaneous, business-component documentation reviewed by human experts matters more than automation or retrospective interviews alone.

Navigating the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 requires corporate finance and tax leaders to balance high-volume data aggregation against rigorous, project-level technical substantiation. While automation resolves the severe administrative time drain of manual data gathering—which a Thomson Reuters compliance blog estimates often exceeds 200 internal hours annually—relying on unverified artificial intelligence to draft technical narratives creates an "audit gap" because Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examiners audit human subject matter experts (SMEs) rather than software. Conversely, traditional consulting and accounting firms provide deep legislative familiarity but rely on retrospective year-end interviews, charge high contingency fees (typically 15% to 30% according to Myriad Associates, and up to 35% at boutique firms according to CPA firm Froehling Anderson) or substantial hourly and study fees ($50,000 to $150,000+ at Big 6 practices according to Boast.ai, and $100,000 to $500,000 at traditional accounting firms according to Thomson Reuters), and frequently bill audit defense separately.
The risks of purely automated, unreviewed AI narratives apply instead to self-service "tech-only" platforms (such as Neo.Tax, MainStreet, or Clarus R+D) or unreviewed AI workflows.
The Evolving IRC Section 41 Compliance and Audit Risk Landscape
Statutory Foundations and the Mandate for Project-Level Substantiation

The federal Research and Experimentation (R&D) tax credit, codified under 26 U.S.C. § 41 (IRC Section 41), provides a general business tax credit designed to incentivize domestic corporate innovation. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2, a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) equal the sum of in-house research expenses—comprising qualified employee wages (for direct conduct, direct supervision, or direct support of research), tangible non-depreciable supplies used in research, and computer rental or cloud hosting costs used directly in research—plus 65% of eligible contract research expenses paid to third parties (or 75% for payments to qualified research consortia and 100% for eligible energy research).

To qualify under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-4, activities must satisfy a strict statutory Four-Part Test, which must be applied separately to each discrete "business component"—defined under § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business:

items: Section 174 / Section 174A Test: The expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures incurred in the experimental or laboratory sense to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Under Section 70302 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025), as reflected in the December 2025 revision of the Form 6765 instructions, IRC Section 174A restored the option for taxpayers to immediately deduct domestic research and experimental expenditures in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, or elect under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize them ratably over at least 60 months, following the 2022–2024 mandatory 5-year domestic and 15-year foreign capitalization regime under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (while foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under amended Section 174, and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 governs transition elections and recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic amounts).

Technological in Nature Test: The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that relies on the principles of the hard sciences, specifically physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Permitted Purpose (Business Component) Test: The application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Process of Experimentation Test: Substantially all—defined quantitatively in regulatory and audit practice as 80% or more—of the research activities for the business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation (such as modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or hypothesis testing) designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to resolve technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. Furthermore, Internal Use Software (IUS) developed for general and administrative (G&A) functions must satisfy an additional three-part High-Threshold-of-Innovation (HTI) Test demonstrating that the software is innovative, its development involves significant economic risk, and it is not commercially available.

body.text: Following initial draft releases in June 2024 and December 2024 (IR-2024-313), the IRS issued the redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / January 2025) alongside updated Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) and subsequent group-reporting clarifications. The redesigned form introduces three major structural sections that transform the return schedule into a narrative and quantitative compliance roadmap. First, Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41) requires filers to report the total number of business components generating QREs (Line 37), the amount of officers' wages included in qualified wages (Line 38), whether any major portion of a trade or business was acquired or disposed of (Line 39), whether new categories of QREs were claimed (Line 40), and whether any QREs were determined under the Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 730 Directive (Line 41, available to taxpayers with assets of $10,000,000 or more preparing certified U.S. GAAP financial statements). Second, Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48) summarizes total qualified wages, supplies, computer rental/lease costs, and applicable contract research across all business components, which must be completed after Section G whenever Section G is required.

Third, Section G (Business Component Information, Lines 49a–56) requires non-exempt taxpayers to itemize each reported business component by controlled group member EIN (Line 49a), principal business activity code (Line 49b), alphanumeric name or unique identifier (Line 49c), component type (Product, Process, or All Others on Line 49d), software category (Internal Use Software [IUS], Dual Function Software [DFS], Excepted from IUS, or Non-IUS on Line 49e), and a narrative description of the information sought to be discovered (Line 49f). For every listed business component, the filer must break down qualified wages into direct research wages (Line 50), direct supervision wages (Line 51), and direct support wages (Line 52), alongside component-specific supplies (Line 54), computer leasing (Line 55), and contract research (Line 56). Under the "80%/Top 50" rule, filers required to complete Section G must itemize business components accounting for a minimum of 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components, reporting any remaining projects in aggregate by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in column 49(c).

While early practitioner commentary (including K-38 Consulting, Cherry Bekaert's January 2025 summary of IR-2024-313, and an October 2025 Thomson Reuters post) cited tax year 2025 as the mandatory start date, the authoritative IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) explicitly establish that for tax years beginning before 2026 (which includes the 2025 tax year), Section G is optional for all filers. Section G becomes required only for tax years beginning after 2025 (i.e., tax year 2026 and later). Moreover, even for tax years beginning after 2025, Section G remains optional for (1) Qualified Small Business (QSB) taxpayers under Section 41(h)(3) electing the payroll tax offset (up to $500,000 under Section D) and (2) taxpayers claiming the research credit on an original return with total controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years of $50 million or less. (Note: Thomson Reuters' October 2025 blog post cited a "$15 million" gross receipts figure, which is superseded by the official IRS gross receipts threshold of $50 million).
Judicial Precedent, Harper v. United States, and Procedural Risk

The IRS's push toward upfront disclosure and project-level substantiation is directly rooted in federal appellate litigation over procedural specificity. Under Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1), a valid claim for credit or refund must satisfy a strict specificity requirement:

"The claim must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof. The statement of the grounds and facts must be verified by a written declaration that it is made under the penalties of perjury. A claim which does not comply with this paragraph will not be considered for any purpose as a claim for refund or credit."

In Harper, Jeffrey Harper, sole shareholder of Harper Construction Co., filed amended R&D tax credit refund claims for tax years 2008 and 2010 and produced over 100,000 pages of documentation during a four-year IRS audit. After denying the claim on the merits at the conclusion of the four-year examination, the government moved to dismiss the taxpayer's refund lawsuit in district court for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under I.R.C. § 7422(a), arguing that the original Form 6765 filings failed to satisfy 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) because they did not identify the specific business components or the employees performing qualified research activities. While the district court agreed with the government and dismissed the complaint, the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the IRS had waived its procedural objection under § 301.6402-2(b)(1) by conducting a four-year substantive examination of the 100,000+ pages of records and issuing a final determination on the merits.

Rather than relaxing enforcement after losing on waiver in Harper, the IRS responded by issuing Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F and IR-2021-203 in October 2021 to ensure that deficient refund claims are rejected procedurally before an audit ever begins (preventing any waiver of § 301.6402-2(b)(1)). Under CCM 20214101F, taxpayers filing R&D refund claims on amended returns were required to provide five items of information at the time of filing: (1) all business components to which the Section 41 credit relates, (2) all research activities performed for each business component, (3) all individuals who performed each research activity, (4) the information each individual sought to discover, and (5) total qualified employee wage, supply, and contract research expenses. Effective June 18, 2024, the IRS updated its refund claim rules (FAQ 21) to waive items (3) and (4)—the names of individuals and the specific information each individual sought to discover—at the initial filing stage for amended returns postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, while extending the 45-day claim perfection period through January 10, 2026. However, taxpayers must still submit items (1), (2), and (5) upfront on amended returns, must produce items (3) and (4) if selected for audit examination, and—for tax years beginning after 2025—must report business component narratives and wage breakdowns directly on original returns via Form 6765 Section G.
The Triple Burden Driving the Need for Technological Efficiency

In this heightened enforcement environment, manual and retrospective R&D study methodologies impose what a September 2025 Thomson Reuters compliance analysis characterizes as the "triple burden" of R&D tax credit compliance: The Time Drain, The Audit Risk, and The Cost Trap. According to Thomson Reuters' blog benchmarks, corporate tax and engineering teams using traditional manual methods often expend over 200 hours annually (and 40 to 60+ hours for mid-market engagements, according to Boast.ai's platform comparison) coordinating retrospective interviews, chasing down fragmented documentation, and validating after-the-fact percentage estimates.

Beyond the internal time drain, Thomson Reuters reports that interview-based retrospective estimates fall short of IRS contemporaneous documentation standards, frequently resulting in audit adjustments that reduce claimed R&D credits by 10% or more while forcing corporate tax departments to maintain higher ASC 740 (FIN 48) uncertain tax position reserves. Conversely, implementing automated ticket-level tracking and contemporaneous cost calculations is reported by Thomson Reuters to yield 20% to 30% lower FIN 48 reserves, save up to 150+ hours of internal compliance effort annually, and deliver 50% to 75% cost savings compared to traditional accounting firm fees. Because traditional accounting firms charge between $100,000 and $500,000 for comprehensive corporate studies according to Thomson Reuters, or $50,000 to $150,000+ for mid-market studies at Big 6 firms according to Boast.ai, continuous technology-enabled data capture has become an economic imperative for preserving the net value of the credit.
Service Model I: Automated and AI-Driven Platforms (Analysis of Boast.ai vs. Tech-Only Tools)
Core Value Proposition: Passive Data Consolidation and Workflow Integration

Through its Boast Time Evidence Engine (BTEE) and enterprise claim platform (which Boast reports is SOC 2 Type II certified), Boast.ai connects directly to source systems to passively and continuously ingest operational evidence throughout the tax year. Specifically, Boast.ai integrates with code repositories and version control systems (GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket to capture code commits, pull requests, and version histories); project management and issue-tracking tools (Jira, Linear, Azure DevOps, Asana, Trello, Monday.com, and ClickUp to capture epics, sprint tickets, timestamps, and worklogs); accounting and ERP platforms (QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, SAP, Workday, Oracle ERP, Sage Intacct, FreshBooks, and Wave to extract general ledger transactions, contractor invoices, and supply expenses); and payroll or HRIS systems (ADP, Gusto, Ceridian, Rippling, BambooHR, and TriNet to map W-2 wages and employee roles to project time allocations).

By synchronizing these technical and financial data streams into a centralized digital audit binder, Boast.ai states on its website that it reduces the internal client time commitment from 60–100+ hours down to approximately 5 hours (or 6–8 hours in earlier small-business press releases).
Boast.ai's Human-Assisted Model vs. Tech-Only Platforms and the AI Audit Gap

Both Boast.ai's primary website documentation and independent third-party competitive analyses (Claimship and GrantOps, updated in 2026) confirm that Boast.ai is not a self-service, software-only tool; rather, it pairs automated AI data ingestion and machine-learning classification with in-house human technical specialists and R&D tax professionals who conduct regular check-ins, write and refine project technical narratives, and file claims end-to-end on the client's behalf. In its own platform comparisons, Boast.ai explicitly differentiates its human-in-the-loop service from self-service "Tech-Only Platforms" (citing Neo.Tax, MainStreet, Clarus R+D, and taxrobot), which rely on self-serve software with minimal or no human expert narrative drafting or audit representation.

As documented in an October 2025 article by MASSIE R&D Tax Credits (Losing the Human Element: Why AI Alone Fails the Audit Test), the IRS does not audit software; it audits people. While generative AI excels at ingesting tickets, organizing data, and drafting structural outlines, MASSIE R&D Tax Credits identifies three acute failure modes when AI is allowed to author Form 6765 technical narratives without rigorous SME verification:

items: Unverified Generic Narratives: AI generates plausible-sounding technical prose (for example, "The team conducted experiments to improve efficiency") that lacks verifiable metrics, specific parameter adjustments, or firsthand context (such as "We ran three iterations of the heat exchange process, adjusting the input temperature by 5°C each time to measure throughput changes. The third test achieved a 12% improvement without increasing energy consumption.").
Terminology and Context Errors: Domain-specific engineering terms are misapplied or disconnected from underlying test logs because no practicing domain expert verified the output.

Erasure of Business Component Distinctions: AI models frequently merge multiple distinct engineering initiatives into a single homogenized summary, destroying the project-by-project boundary required by 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and Form 6765 Section G.

body.text: Because IRS examiners are trained to spot boilerplate AI text, they prioritize live, interactive conversations during an audit, asking engineering leads how uncertainties were identified, requesting specific examples of failed and successful test iterations, and cross-checking oral testimony against contemporaneous logs. In a case example reported by MASSIE R&D Tax Credits, a software company relied entirely on AI to draft its Form 6765 technical narratives; during the ensuing IRS examination, the lead engineer—who had neither drafted nor reviewed the AI text—could not explain the generic technical uncertainty section in meaningful detail, prompting the IRS to disallow two projects for insufficient technical detail. Furthermore, according to Boast.ai's platform comparison analysis of pure self-service algorithms, fully automated "black box" platforms miss 25% to 40% of qualifying R&D activities on average (such as indirect supervision/support wages or subtle process improvements).
Audit Defense (AuditShield) and Pricing Structure Correction

Under AuditShield, Boast's in-house tax specialists represent the client throughout IRS or Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) examinations, claiming on its website to reduce audit preparation time by up to 90% and achieve an audit win rate 2x the industry average.

Boast.ai's platform comparison and third-party competitor benchmarks (Claimship and GrantOps) confirm that Boast.ai does not publish a flat SaaS subscription tier; instead, it charges a value-based success (contingency) fee calculated as a percentage of the tax credit value delivered, quoted per customer via an order form. While Boast's terms stipulate that its fee reduces proportionally if a claim is cut in an audit and refunds in full if rejected—and while Boast estimates its total fees typically run 40% to 60% lower than Big 6 accounting firms—its percentage-of-credit pricing scales directly with claim size, unlike fixed-fee or flat-subscription models.
Service Model II: Traditional Accounting and Boutique R&D Consulting Firms
Core Value Proposition: Legislative Mastery and High-Touch Service

Boutique specialists, in particular, offer a comprehensive, hands-off service experience in which consultants conduct team interviews, gather financial records, author technical project reports, and prepare tax return schedules.
Operational Inefficiencies and the Flaws of Retrospective Reconstruction

Despite their legislative expertise, traditional accounting and consulting firms rely heavily on manual, retrospective workflows—engaging with the client months after the close of the tax year to reconstruct R&D activities through memory-based interviews and spreadsheet exports. First, it imposes a heavy internal time drain and slow study turnaround. While UK consultancy Myriad Associates notes that small, hands-off boutique claims can require as little as 4 to 6 hours of client input, U.S. mid-market and enterprise benchmarks from Thomson Reuters and Boast.ai state that traditional manual studies require 40 to 60+ hours—and often over 200 hours annually—of internal coordination, engineering interviews, and spreadsheet validation. Second, reconstructing technical uncertainties and employee time percentages via year-end oral interviews directly conflicts with the IRS's expectation of contemporaneous documentation organized by business component.
Fee Structures, Circular 230 Constraints, and Financial Risk Misalignment

In the U.S. market, CPA firm Froehling Anderson documents in its R&D Tax Credit eBook that boutique R&D firms typically charge a contingent fee of 35% of the R&D credits generated. Tying a consultant's compensation directly to the size of the credit creates an inherent conflict of interest that incentivizes aggressive QRE inflation. Furthermore, as Moss Adams explains, IRS Circular 230 prohibits tax practitioners from charging contingent fees for R&D tax credit return preparation. Some providers attempt to circumvent Circular 230 by charging hourly rates subject to a "fee cap" tied to anticipated credits; Moss Adams notes that this often results in higher effective hourly rates, less work performed, and no refund of fees if the IRS disallows the credit during an audit.

Conversely, traditional Big 6 and generalist CPA firms bill on a time-and-materials (hourly) or fixed-fee basis, charging $50,000 to $150,000+ for mid-market studies according to Boast.ai and $100,000 to $500,000 for large corporate studies according to Thomson Reuters. Critically, as verified by Moss Adams, Froehling Anderson, and Boast.ai, traditional accounting firms and fixed-fee engagements generally exclude audit defense from the initial preparation fee, billing examination representation separately at standard or premium hourly rates only if and when an IRS audit occurs. While boutique contingency firms often build audit defense into their 15%–35% contingent fee, Froehling Anderson points out that this forces clients to pay an expensive audit-defense fee every year even when audits are infrequent.
Service Model III: The Integrated Hybrid Ecosystem (TaxTrex)
Institutionalized Conservatism, Specialist Heritage, and ISO Governance

Second, the firm is certified to the ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management) standard, governing its Information Security Management System (ISMS) to ensure encrypted, access-controlled, and logged protection of sensitive client intellectual property, source code, and financial records.
Technological Backbone: TaxTrex ($375/Month), 90-Minute Processing, and Substantiation Tracker

It pairs with the Substantiation Tracker, a dedicated compliance tool that enables project staff to perform real-time logging of employee R&D time and organize technical artifacts (such as Git logs, Jira tickets, CAD drawings, and failure logs) by business component.

Furthermore, TaxTrex integrates directly with leading accounting software to sync general ledger and payroll records with R&D activities, while structurally embedding the IRC Section 41 Four-Part Test ("entity density and compliance") to generate audit-ready technical narratives, R&D tax substantiation position papers, and Form 6765 schedules. Commercially, TaxTrex is offered under a B2B subscription model starting at a fixed tier of $375/month ($4,500 annually), with tiered access permissions for internal finance staff, engineers, contractors, and external business advisers, and supports international R&D tax compliance across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and Singapore.
The Human Compliance Gateway: The Mandatory Six-Eye Review

items: First Set of Eyes — The Qualified Engineer: Reviews the technical data compiled by TaxTrex (including software architecture diagrams, Git commit histories, Jira tickets, CAD files, and trial logs) and conducts targeted technical verification to ensure the narrative accurately reflects engineering reality and satisfies the Section 41 Four-Part Test. If a project lacks testing logs or version history demonstrating technical uncertainty, the engineer flags it as high-risk.

Second Set of Eyes — The Scientist: Evaluates the research methodology to confirm adherence to the scientific method (Hypothesis → Test → Analyze → Refine). The scientist distinguishes eligible systematic experimentation from routine quality control or post-production debugging, rejecting claims that show only a final result without iterative data (such as lab notes or failed prototypes) needed to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" threshold.

Third Set of Eyes — The CPA or Enrolled Agent: Verifies the financial calculations, ties QRE schedules back to the general ledger and W-2 payroll registers, excludes non-qualified fringe benefits (such as employer 401(k) contributions and health insurance premiums), checks supply versus depreciable asset classifications, and ensures compliance with IRC Section 41, Section 174A, and Form 6765 instructions.

body.text: Financial De-Risking: Fee Transparency and the creditARMOR Conflict Resolution

Instead, in addition to the $375/month TaxTrex subscription, the firm offers three non-contingent engagement models. First, its Fixed-Fee Engagement uses a flat, pre-agreed rate based on estimated hours, technical complexity, and scope to provide upfront budget certainty (and includes a "No Benefit, No Charge" protection where no fee is charged if no tax benefit is received). Second, its Phased / Hybrid Model structures fees by project milestones (such as scoping, technical writing, and financial calculation) or combines scheduled hourly rates with fixed-fee options to manage cash flow on complex, multi-year claims. Third, its Hourly Consulting (Time Billing) model bills standard hourly rates of $195 to $395 per hour for ad-hoc advisory, Information Document Request (IDR) responses, or audit defense representation.

"creditARMOR is not an insurance policy... creditARMOR does not offer an insurance policy, reimbursement benefit, or financial indemnity. There is no promise to pay financial losses or provide services upon the occurrence of a future audit."

In accordance with legal weight principles—where specific contractual service terms and formal legal disclaimers govern over general promotional summaries—taxpayers and CFOs must treat creditARMOR as a free AI-powered mock audit simulation and pre-filing risk-management software platform, not an indemnity insurance policy. Specifically, creditARMOR evaluates federal and 38 state R&D credit programs (39 programs total) through a 4-step mock examination workflow:

items: Step 1 (Upload Claim Forms): Ingests federal Form 6765, state claim forms, and prior-year returns, automatically extracting business components listed in Section G.

Step 2 (Add Supporting Evidence): Tracks uploaded documentation across 11 evidence categories (payroll and wage records, time tracking/allocation, project records and technical specifications, test logs and results, contracts and SOWs, calculations, claim forms and prior-year forms, locations and states, Form 6765 readiness, and TaxTrex position papers).

Step 3 (Draft IDR Questions & Multi-AI Cross-Check): Generates 1-to-2-page draft Information Document Request (IDR) examiner questions and answers per project, cross-checked by multiple AI models and rated Strong, Weak, or Missing against the uploaded evidence.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: Form 6765 Credit Calculation and Net Retention Across Provider Models
Step 1: Hypothetical Taxpayer Profile and Form 6765 Section G and Section F QRE Breakdown

Assume a hypothetical mid-market U.S. software company, VectorGrid Software Corp., files an original corporate income tax return for Tax Year 2026 (beginning January 1, 2026). Because Tax Year 2026 begins after December 31, 2025, and VectorGrid's QREs exceed $1.5 million, Section G of Form 6765 is mandatory. VectorGrid conducts qualified research across 6 software business components and incurs the following categories of QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b):

items: Direct research wages (Form 6765, Section G, Line 50): $1,800,000.
Direct supervision wages (Form 6765, Section G, Line 51): $300,000.
Direct support wages (Form 6765, Section G, Line 52): $100,000.
Total qualified wages (Section G, Line 53 and Section F, Line 42): $1,800,000 + $300,000 + $100,000 = $2,200,000.
Cost of tangible, non-depreciable research supplies (Section F, Line 43 and Section G, Line 54): $50,000.
Rental or lease cost of computers / development cloud hosting (Section F, Line 44 and Section G, Line 55): $120,000.

Contract research expenses (Section F, Line 45 and Section G, Line 56): VectorGrid pays $200,000 to an unrelated U.S. engineering contractor for qualified research. Applying the statutory 65% inclusion rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) yields $200,000 × 0.65 = $130,000.
Total Current-Year QREs (Form 6765, Section F, Line 48): $2,200,000 + $50,000 + $120,000 + $130,000 = $2,500,000.

body.text: Under the Section G "80%/Top 50" rule, VectorGrid must individually itemize business components representing at least 80% of its $2,500,000 total QREs ($2,500,000 × 0.80 = $2,000,000). VectorGrid itemizes its top 4 software business components (which account for $2,150,000, or 86% of total QREs) on separate lines in Section G, and reports the remaining 2 components ($350,000, or 14%) on a single line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in column 49(c).
Step 2: Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) and Section 280C Calculation (Form 6765, Section B)
Assume VectorGrid elects the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under Section B of Form 6765 and had prior-year QREs of $1,900,000 in 2023, $2,000,000 in 2024, and $2,100,000 in 2025:

items: Line 20 (Current-Year Total QREs from Line 48): $2,500,000.
Line 21 (Total QREs for Prior 3 Tax Years): $1,900,000 + $2,000,000 + $2,100,000 = $6,000,000.

Line 26 (Net ASC with IRC Section 280C Reduced Credit Election — Line 25 Multiplied by 79% [0.79]): To avoid reducing its Section 174A domestic research deduction by the $210,000 gross credit, VectorGrid elects the reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c) on Header Item A, multiplying Line 25 by 79% (0.79) (reflecting the 21% maximum corporate tax rate reduction) to yield $210,000 × 0.79 = $165,900.

body.text: Step 3: Net Financial Benefit Comparison Across Service Models (Initial Filing vs. Audit Examination)

Comparing VectorGrid's net retained cash benefit from the $165,900 net Section 280C tax credit (and $210,000 gross credit) across the provider models demonstrates how pricing structures and audit adjustments impact net taxpayer retention:

items: Scenario A — TaxTrex Hybrid Model: Pre-audit, VectorGrid subscribes to TaxTrex at the fixed tier of $375/month ($375 × 12 = $4,500/year), which includes a complimentary Six-Eye Review. Total upfront expenditure equals $4,500 + $11,800 = $16,300, allowing VectorGrid to retain $165,900 - $16,300 = $149,600 (90.17% of the net Section 280C credit).

Scenario B — Boast.ai (Automated Platform + In-House Specialists + AuditShield): Pre-audit, Boast.ai charges a value-based success fee that it estimates runs 40% to 60% lower than Big 6 accounting firm fees. Using the 50% midpoint reduction relative to a $100,000 Big 6 study, Boast.ai's fee is $50,000 (representing 23.81% of the $210,000 gross credit), requiring approximately 5 hours of internal staff time. VectorGrid retains $165,900 - $50,000 = $115,900 (69.86% of the net 280C credit). Post-audit, AuditShield representation is included at no extra cost. Applying Boast.ai's self-reported benchmark of recovering 95% of the estimated credit (0.95 × $165,900 = $157,605, an $8,295 disallowance) and its contractual term reducing its fee proportionally by 5% (0.95 × $50,000 = $47,500), VectorGrid retains $157,605 - $47,500 = $110,105 (66.37% of the original net 280C credit).

Scenario C — Traditional Boutique Consulting Firm (30% to 35% Contingency Fee): Pre-audit, charging a 30% contingency fee (the upper bound of Myriad Associates' 15%–30% range) on the $210,000 gross credit costs $210,000 × 0.30 = $63,000, leaving $165,900 - $63,000 = $102,900 (62.03% net retention). At the 35% contingency fee documented by Froehling Anderson, the fee is $210,000 × 0.35 = $73,500, leaving VectorGrid with $165,900 - $73,500 = $92,400 (55.70% of the net 280C credit). Post-audit, if reliance on retrospective year-end interviews results in the 10% credit reduction cited by Thomson Reuters, the net 280C credit drops by $16,590 to $149,310. Under a capped/non-refundable $73,500 fee arrangement, VectorGrid retains $149,310 - $73,500 = $75,810 (45.70% of the original net credit), and the effective fee-to-benefit ratio rises to $73,500 / $149,310 = 49.23% (before any separate hourly audit defense charges).

Scenario D — Traditional Big 6 Accounting Firm ($100,000 Study + Separate Audit Billing): Pre-audit, at the lower bound of Thomson Reuters' $100,000 to $500,000 traditional accounting firm fee range (and the midpoint of Boast.ai's $50,000 to $150,000+ Big 6 benchmark), VectorGrid pays $100,000 and expends 60 to 200+ hours of internal engineering and tax staff time, retaining $165,900 - $100,000 = $65,900 (39.72%). Post-audit, even if the conservative Big 6 study sustains 100% of the $165,900 credit, audit defense is billed separately at hourly rates. Adding $15,000 in separate hourly examination defense fees reduces VectorGrid's net retained benefit to $165,900 - $115,000 = $50,900 (30.68%).

body.text: Strategic Recommendations for Corporate R&D Tax Compliance

items: Eliminate Purely Retrospective and Unreviewed AI Workflows: With Form 6765 Section G becoming mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (for claimants above the $1.5M QRE / $50M gross receipts small-filer exception) and IRS examiners testing whether engineering leads can substantiate project-level uncertainties in live interviews, both year-end memory-based reconstruction and unreviewed "tech-only" AI narrative generation carry substantial disallowance risk. Continuous, year-round digital evidence capture tied directly to business components is now the baseline expectation for IRC Section 41 compliance.

Consider Boast.ai When Cross-Border North American Automation and Bundled Audit Representation Fit a Value-Based Budget: For software, gaming, and high-growth technology companies operating across the United States and Canada that prefer an automated, low-lift (~5 hours internal time) full-service engagement with included AuditShield representation and early non-dilutive funding advances, Boast.ai provides a substantially more automated and integrated alternative to traditional consulting—provided leadership accounts for its percentage-based success fee structure.

Prioritize the TaxTrex Integrated Hybrid Model for Net Credit Retention, Multi-Disciplinary Defensibility, and Governance Certainty: Combining TaxTrex ($375/month, 90-minute AI compilation) and the Substantiation Tracker with the mandatory Six-Eye Review (Engineer, Scientist, and CPA/Enrolled Agent), pre-filing creditARMOR mock audit stress-testing, ISO 31000 / ISO 27001 accreditation, and non-contingent fixed or hourly ($195–$395/hr) pricing resolves the tension between technological speed and human expert defensibility while preserving a larger share of the tax credit for corporate innovation.
